claim: In 2019 the first hull was found cracked, making it incapable of reaching the Titanic; the first Director of Engineering testified his refusal to sign off blocked it from the 2019 expedition and led to his firing; fired 26 JUL 2019; Rush's 16 JUL 2019 letter cited the expedition's cancellation
source_quote: a crack found in the carbon fiber hull of the first TITAN, which rendered it incapable of reaching the depths of the TITANIC | his refusal to sign off on the first TITAN hull due to damage and concerning RTM data successfully blocked its participation in OceanGate’s scheduled 2019 TITANIC Expedition | his refusal to sign off on the hull angered Mr. Rush and led to the termination of his employment | On July 26, 2019, OceanGate fired the Director of Engineering. | Due to unforeseen circumstances leading to the cancellation of the TITANIC Survey Expedition 2019
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/); 4.22.23.1, 4.22.24.1 (PDF p. 164) and 5.19 (PDF p. 320). His account as his testimony; the company's letter beside it

claim: Brooks, a software engineer, was promoted to Director of Engineering over the winter before the 2022 expedition
source_quote: Over the course of the winter prior to TITANIC Expedition 2022, OceanGate’s Director of Engineering was fired and an existing member (software engineer) of the OceanGate team was promoted to Director of Engineering.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/); 4.34.1, PDF p. 231. That the promoted engineer is Brooks: CG 112 (his testimony); fact-check to confirm

claim: Brooks: the post-dive-80 hull inspection was limited (insert inside, covered outside; a flashlight down a small gap, 'not a great test'); the insert was never removed; a sudden shift in level is 'something to be concerned about, for sure'; he is not a strain or materials expert
source_url: https://www.news.uscg.mil/News-by-Region/Headquarters/Titan-Submersible/ (CG 112, MBI Formal Hearing and Post Hearing Transcripts Combined)
source_quote: we did an inspection of the hull as best we could, but it's hard because there's the insert on the inside and then, of course, it's covered on the outside | a sudden shift in level was something that -- that's something to be concerned about, for sure | I'm not necessarily a strain expert or materials expert | I know we definitely did not take the insert out because that was never done. | you can take a flashlight and you can -- there's a small gap between the insert and the hull | it's not a great test
note: CG 112 p. 764-765 of 1651 (Brooks, sworn)

claim: Brooks: after dive 81 'we didn't see any further shifts in strain data, you know, no loud bangs, no -- nothing with the AE that really seemed out of the ordinary'
source_url: https://www.news.uscg.mil/News-by-Region/Headquarters/Titan-Submersible/ (CG 112, MBI Formal Hearing and Post Hearing Transcripts Combined)
source_quote: we didn't really see anything, we didn't see any further shifts in strain data, you know, no loud bangs, no -- nothing with the AE that really seemed out of the ordinary
note: CG 112 p. 764 of 1651 (Brooks, sworn)

claim: Brooks: AE sensor 4 showed activity on dives 81-83 of the kind they wanted to be concerned about but never crossed the 5,000 threshold they had set; it never got worse, so he did not think it was a concern
source_url: https://www.news.uscg.mil/News-by-Region/Headquarters/Titan-Submersible/ (CG 112, MBI Formal Hearing and Post Hearing Transcripts Combined)
source_quote: sensor 4 did have a characteristic of the kind of thing that we wanted to be concerned about, but it was never really that high | crossing that 5,000 threshold that we had determined | because it never -- it never got worse and, like I said, it was never -- it never went beyond the threshold, then I don't think it was a concern
note: CG 112 p. 763 of 1651 (Brooks, sworn). Units of the threshold not stated: never say a unit

claim: A contractor (Antonella Wilby) testified she asked Brooks whether the data could indicate delamination; in her account he said it was only a few microns, the next two dives on mission 5 would go ahead, with a visual inspection back in Seattle; she flew home the next day
source_url: https://www.news.uscg.mil/News-by-Region/Headquarters/Titan-Submersible/ (CG 112, MBI Formal Hearing and Post Hearing Transcripts Combined)
source_quote: I did bring up delamination to Phil as, you know, could that have been something indicated in these data, and he said, well, it was only a few microns. | we'll do the next two dives on mission 5 and when it gets back to Seattle, we'll do a visual inspection. | So, I flew home the next day
note: CG 112 p. 1403 of 1651 (sworn). Her account: attributed in the VO ('in her account'); USCG ROI 4.34 (PDF p. 234) records it as 'reportedly'. Brooks's response to this point not found in CG 112: fairness pass to search. Not named on air

claim: The USCG board: leaving the Director of Engineering post vacant for 2023 removed the possibility of a replacement Director blocking the expedition, given that the first Director of Engineering's refusal had blocked the hull in 2019
source_quote: his decision to leave the Director of Engineering position vacant for the 2023 operating season removed the possibility of a replacement Director blocking the expedition or raising concerns with OceanGate’s Board of Directors.
note: USCG MBI ROI 04 AUG 2025 (official file, Drive titan/records/); 5.19, PDF p. 320. The board's analysis, said as the board's

claim: Under US law a submersible under 100 GT carrying at least one passenger for hire is a small passenger vessel subject to USCG inspection; OceanGate did not register or document Titan nor arrange a USCG inspection
source_quote: because OceanGate operated the Titan with passengers for hire, it was required to be inspected by the US Coast Guard | However, OceanGate did not register or document the Titan in the United States, nor did they arrange to have it inspected by the US Coast Guard.
note: NTSB 2.6, PDF p. 67-68 and fn 48

claim: USCG NVIC 05-93 (July 1993) was never updated after the Passenger Vessel Safety Act of 1993 (signed December 1993) changed the definition to any submersible with one passenger for hire; the USCG has no specific inspection standards for submersible design or construction
source_quote: In July 1993, the US Coast Guard published NVIC 05-93 | After the Passenger Vessel Safety Act of 1993 was signed into law, the definition of a small passenger vessel changed to include any submersible carrying at least one passenger for hire. | The NVIC has not been updated since its release to reflect this change, and the US Coast Guard does not have specific inspection standards for the design or construction of submersibles
note: NTSB 1.8.2 and 2.6, PDF p. 56-57, 68-69. PVSA signed December 1993 (NTSB 1.8.2: 'signed into law in December 1993')

claim: NVIC 05-93 recommended restricting operations to the depth rescue assistance could reach; Titan regularly dived beyond 45 m and without rescue assistance on standby capable of reaching it at the Titanic
source_quote: the NVIC recommended restricting submersible operations to waters less than a submersible’s rated depth or the “depth to which its rescue assistance is effective | The Titan regularly dove beyond 45 meters, and OceanGate regularly operated the Titan without rescue assistance on standby and capable of reaching the submersible while it dove to the Titanic wreckage
note: NTSB 2.6, PDF p. 68

claim: USCG board: a seven-hour initial notification delay dictated by OceanGate's communications plan; no backup deep-water assets; NTSB: had OceanGate followed NVIC 05-93 it would likely have had assets standing by and Titan likely found sooner, even though a rescue was not possible
source_quote: Despite a seven-hour initial notification delay dictated by OceanGate's communications plan | had OceanGate followed NVIC 05-93 guidance for emergency response plans, they likely would have had emergency response assets standing by and the Titan likely would have been found sooner, saving time and resources even though a rescue was not possible in this case
note: USCG ROI 5.21 PDF p. 324; NTSB 2.5 / finding 7. Note: ROI 4.1.65 gives 7:10 p.m. as about 7 h 23 min after the last communication, while the last message was 10:47 a.m. (likely different time zones): say 'about seven hours' as the board's count only

source_quote: Revise Navigation and Vessel Inspection Circular 05-93 to include the revised definition of small passenger vessel as reflected in the Passenger Vessel Safety Act of 1993
